Knysna Revisited - Update

By: Catherine Rice | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Our recent update on the failed attempt to place Knysna under administration generated a significant response, notably from residents who opposed the move.

Unique Selling Point:
Our recent update on the failed attempt to place Knysna under administration generated a significant response, notably from residents who opposed the move. They felt our update didn't provide a full picture, so we returned to Knysna to get their views. Last month, the National Council of Provinces blocked the Western Cape provincial government's move to dissolve Knysna's council and appoint an administrator.

Summary:
On September 12, the Western Cape DA provincial government tabled a notice of dissolution of the Knysna Local Municipality, and planned to appoint an administrator in a bid to restore service delivery. Western Cape MEC for local government Anton Bredell said the decision was due to protracted and ongoing systemic governance and service delivery failures. But, the decision was ultimately blocked by the NCOP on September the 26th. Knysna is governed by an ANC-led coalition with the PA, PBI and EFF.

In Knysna, the Democratic Alliance supported the plan to place the town under administration, but all other parties represented on the municipal council, including the Knysna Independent Movement (KIM), opposed it.

The town has been plagued by political infighting and service delivery failures for years. The ANC led coalition has been in power since August 2022. Former ANC Mayor, Aubrey Tsengwa, has been blamed for many of the problems, and some residents say the town finally has stability under new ANC Mayor Thando Matika. He took office at the end of February.

Knysna Infrastructure Group, an apolitical organisation trying to assist the Municipality to restore service delivery, believes Matika needs to be given a chance to turn things around. KIG's Eugene Vermaak believes placing the town under administration would have been disruptive and would have triggered further political instability.

Carte Blanche visited Knysna in February 2024 when the town was showing visible signs of collapse. A decomposing body had been found in one of the reservoirs just weeks before our visit, in December 2023. Sewage spills were common, and refuse collection was non-existent resulting in a rat infestation in the centre of town. When we returned to do another story in June 2025, we found a town still struggling with service delivery failures. But, many were opposed to the town being placed under administration, arguing Knysna was being used as a pawn in a political game, and that the new Mayor needed time to resolve the issues.

Further information:
Furthermore, AfriForum also welcomed the decision of the National Council of Provinces to reject the proposal to place the Knysna Local Municipality under administration. It said the plan to place Knysna under administration was not about improving service delivery, but about political control.

Script:


VO 1 Saturday afternoon - the 11th of October.

VO 2 A fire has broken out in Knysna’s CBD..

VO 3 Informal structures built illegally next to the Waste Transfer Station -razed to the ground.

VO 4 We’re visiting Knysna for the third time in less than two years.

VO 5 To find out.. if this iconic town has become collateral damage in the politcal fight to control it?

UPSOUND (in Afrikaans) Since last night, we haven't had any water. We struggle with water and power. Look at how the people come here for water.

FADE TO BLACK

NATSOUND Yoh guys this is very very bad. It’s a manhole overflowing, it’s been over two months. Very bad for the kids.

VO 6 Raw sewage spills have become routine, flowing into one of South Africa’s most sensitive estuaries.

VO 7 Ageing infrastructure has not kept pace with a growing population - now at around 100,000 residents.

VO 8 For years, it's been in a downward spiral - without the funds or political will to resolve the problems.

VO 9 The town is run by a coalition led by the ANC. But last month, in what it called a last resort, the Western Cape Provincial Government resolved to place the town under administration - effectively dissolving its municipal council. It was a decision ultimately blocked by Parliament’s National Council of Provinces, or NCOP, which has the power to veto such decisions.

NATSOUND: Seven provinces had voted in favour of the report, whilst two provinces, they voted against the report.

VO 10 In a statement, Local Government MEC, Anton Bredell said the NCOP’s decision meant additional funds that would have been unlocked will no longer be available.

VO 11 He added that his hands are now tied. (show part of statement on screen)

UPSOUND Lynn Kaster / Community Activist: They are using Knysna as a pawn for power and we don’t want that because that is not for the people.

VO 12 Lynn Kaster is a community activist. We met her back in February 2024. She believes Knysna has become the sacrificial lamb in the fight between the ANC and the DA.

CR: What do you think about the situation in Knysna now, now that it wasn’t put under administration?

UPSOUND Lynn Kaster / Community Activist: Well, I was very much involved in protesting against putting this municipality under administration. Everything is chaotic when there’s new elections and things like that. New money means new tenders, new contractors and its chaos, and then service delivery stands still for quite a while.

VO 13 Kaster says Knysna’s Council is now stable, and is making strides.

UPSOUND Lynn Kaster: A few months ago, a year ago, it was chaos, it was terrible. I didn’t see us coming out of this but with the recent shuffle with the old Mayor out and the new Mayor , I’ve seen them cover so much ground. Electricians are back, we’ve got two female engineers in the electrical department, a new manager, we’ve got directors in all posts.

VO 14 But, it’s clear there’s still a long way to go. We’ve been here for less than twelve hours and in that time the Knysna Muncipality’s whatsapp channel sends out a string of notifications to residents. There are technical issues with the emergency services phone lines, a power outage, a problem with water supply, a burst water pipe.

NATSOUND: Not two burst sewer manholes, but three in Dikkop and this one right outside a nursery school.

VO 15 On Sunday morning, we wake up to an overcast sky, with intermittent rain.The main street looks run down and depressing.

VO 16 And we receive news that parts of Hornlee are without water - once again.

VO 17 A water truck makes its way through the suburb.

UPSOUND Machel Christians / Hornlee Resident: (in Afrikaans) They say it’s just this area without water. Just outside Hornlee, there is water. They’re comfortable. We’re not.

VO 18 Residents we speak to are divided on whether the town should have been placed under administration, but all agree service delivery failures impact their everyday lives.

UPSOUND Rosa Levack / Knysna Resident: (in Afrikaans) Yesterday, we didn't have electricity or water - both of them. And it’s a struggle.
UPSOUND Jeff Milachowski / Knysna Resident:: I’m sad because we’ve got such a beautiful town and we have to live like we’re living now, without water, without electricity, without decent tar roads.
UPSOUND: Willem Danhaus / Knysna Resident: It’s not what we deserve, that they press us down. Very unhappy. It’s not a pleasure to live here anymore.
UPSOUND Robert Winn / Knysna Resident: I really think dissolution should have happened. We need intervention and we need major intervention. We need to remove half the problem to address the rest of the problem.

VO 19 It will now fall to civil society organisations, like the Knysna Infrastructure Group, to turn things around.

VO 20 But, without significant funding there is only so much they can do.

VO 21 Eugene Vermaak is one of the Group’s founders. It raises funds to support the Municipality.

UPSOUND Eugene Vermaak / Knysna Infrastructure Group: The Knysna Infrastructure Group on our own we can never do this. We’ve got some funding from about 820 residents. 820 residents is not going to save or make a total impact. We need some serious funding. And that funding, there is an obligation on national, provincial to all play a role in that funding role, and then we can definitely make a major impact.

VO 22 He says the Western Cape government should have looked at other alternatives – assisting with administration, but not dissolving council.

UPSOUND Eugene Vermaak: The administrator is appointed to take over the physical day to day management of the council so they take over the management structure, the execution level and they will then in that case be able to capacitate, bring extra people in, bring the resources in, be able to fund it, and there’s no limit in terms of how long that administrator can be there.

VO 23 He believes negative perceptions are being reinforced for political gain. Like the fact that a decomposing body was found in a reservoir almost two years ago.

UPSOUND Eugene Vermaak: That decomposed body in the reservoir was on the 26th of November 2023. It’s not now, not 2025 so any reference to that for lower standards because we had a body in the reservoir two years later, I think is wrong.

VO 24 We visit the reservoir where the body was found to see if security has been beefed up since then … it hasn’t.

VO 25 At the waste transfer station, rubbish has been removed – an improvement after our last visit.

VO 26 And drinking tap water is apparently safe.

UPSOUND Eugene Vermaak: All of us in this town drink it out of the tap. There’s no cholera , no gastro because of the water quality we’re drinking. Do we have problems? Yes. There are areas in this lagoon that is contaminated with excessive ecoli, we are working flat out to fix that.

VO 27 But he says most of the lagoon is now swimmable.

CR Do you think its a town still worth visiting?

UPSOUND Eugene Vermaak: My answer to people who are watching and visitors who want to come to Knysna, hell yes, we’re open. Look for yourself.

VO 28 As our weekend in Knysna draws to a close, the sun comes out again. I hope that when we return it’ll be to tell the story of a town that has beaten the odds, and reclaimed its title: jewel of the Garden Route.
